Title: Prioritizing Saving Lives: The Imperative for a Mandatory Post-Mortem Organ Donation Policy

Introduction

The gift of life extends beyond our earthly days into the legacy we leave behind. By opting for a mandatory post-mortem organ donation policy, devoid of the need for individual or family consent, society can significantly amplify the continuity of life through the miraculous process of transplantation. This essay advocates for the implementation of such a policy, arguing that the urgent need to maximize the availability of transplantable organs should outweigh concerns about post-death bodily autonomy. The potential to save and enhance countless lives, reduce the economic burden on healthcare systems, and foster a culture of altruism underscores the necessity of this policy shift.

Maximizing Organ Availability: A Life-or-Death Imperative

Organ transplantation is a beacon of modern medical science, offering hope and restoration to individuals suffering from terminal organ diseases. The demand for donor organs far outstrips the supply, creating a grim reality where countless lives are lost each year due to the unavailability of vital organs. Countries with opt-in (voluntary) donation systems frequently struggle with low donation rates, inadvertently condemning a segment of the populace to premature death. A mandatory donation system, on the other hand, ensures that every eligible individual is a donor, significantly increasing the pool of available organs.

Such a policy does not arbitrarily infringe on personal liberties; rather, it prioritizes the greater good. The human body, post-mortem, loses its sentinel functions and, in the absence of explicit donor status, might be destined to decompose in solitude, a squandered potential for healing and renewal. By mandating organ donation, we honor the principle that the most profound respect for the deceased is the continuation of their beneficence in the form of a new life.

Bodily Autonomy vs. End-of-Life Choice

Proponents of bodily autonomy may argue that the decision to donate should remain a personal choice, reflecting an individual’s values and cultural beliefs. However, this argument is predicated on the assumption that one’s bodily integrity extends into the afterlife—a time deemed inconsequential if devoid of consciousness. The essence of bodily autonomy should not unduly trump the altruistic potential of the dead.

Moreover, consent for organ donation can be obtained pre-mortem through universal registration systems, ensuring that individuals are aware of their choice, if any, prior to their demise. Thus, the policy does not entirely dispense with individual preference but places it at a manageable distance from the immediacy of death. This approach respects the autonomy of life while answering the clear moral obligation to save others post-life.

Economic and Social Benefits

The implementation of a mandatory organ donation policy also bears substantial economic benefits. The costs associated with organ transplantation, including surgical procedures, immunosuppressive therapies, and post-operative care, are significant. However, the indirect benefits—significantly reduced long-term healthcare expenditures due to decreased disability and increased productivity among transplant recipients—are monumental. Furthermore, a society that adopts such a policy can lead the charge in reducing healthcare disparities, as organ scarcity is often exacerbated by systemic inequities.

Beyond economics, fostering a culture where life-saving organ donation is a seamless extension of dying necessitates a collective moral framework valuing selflessness over personal end-of-life decisions. This societal shift encourages open discourse on life, death, and the profound impact of individual choices on communal welfare, reinforcing a more empathetic, interconnected society.

Addressing Ethical Considerations and Counterarguments

Critics may raise concerns about the potential for coercion or disrespect for cultural traditions that oppose organ donation. However, these fears are mitigated by a framework that includes a universal pre-mortem registry, allowing individuals to opt-out if they wish, albeit at a broader societal cost. The policy should be accompanied by comprehensive education programs to dispel misconceptions about organ donation, emphasizing that it is a noble, life-affirming act.

Furthermore, objections based on a perceived violation of the sacredness of the dead overlook the fact that the dead body, bereft of consciousness, offers an unprecedented opportunity to serve as a vessel of healing and hope. The dignity of the deceased is preserved not in withholding from transplantation but in ensuring their legacy through the survival and flourishing of another.

Conclusion

In the calculus of life and death, the imperative to save lives through organ transplantation outweighs the legacy of individual or familial consent post-mortem. A mandatory organ donation policy, underpinned by universal pre-mortem registration and devoid of end-of-life decision-making hurdles, promises to increase the availability of vital organs, alleviate the economic and social burdens of organ shortage, and cultivate a culture of altruism and empathy. By embracing this policy, society not only extends the gift of life to many but also upholds a profound moral duty to honor the legacy of those who have departed by ensuring their final act is one of giving, not taking. The time is ripe for a paradigm shift in organ donation practices, prioritizing the sanctity of life in its most transformative form—through the transplantation of hope.

Title: The Ultimate Gift, Mandated: Why Presumed Consent Must Override Bodily Autonomy in Death

In the sterile quiet of an operating room, a surgeon’s scalpel pauses. Across town, a twenty-three-year-old mother of two lies tethered to a dialysis machine, her blood cycling through a filter that cannot replace a living kidney. Sixty miles away, a grandfather’s breath grows shallower as his name inches up a list he may not live to see the top of. Every day, seventeen people in the United States die waiting for an organ transplant. This is not an unavoidable tragedy of nature; it is a systemic failure of policy. We have the medical ability to save these lives, yet we prioritize the absolute autonomy of a corpse over the beating heart of a living person. The moral calculus is clear: a mandatory, post-mortem organ donation policy—one that does not require individual or family consent—is not only justified but ethically essential.

The primary argument against such a policy—that it violates bodily autonomy—rests on a fundamental category error. Bodily autonomy is a vital principle for the living, protecting individuals from unwanted medical intrusion and violation of their personhood. But a dead body is not a person. It is a biological vessel. To grant a corpse the same inviolable rights as a living, sentient human being is to fetishize tissue over consciousness. A person who dies leaving behind a healthy heart, liver, and corneas does not experience the "violation" of their removal. They are beyond suffering. However, the patient dying of pulmonary fibrosis or the child in end-stage renal failure experiences the agony of waiting and the finality of death. By elevating the preferences of a non-experiencing entity over the urgent needs of a living, breathing human, we have inverted our ethical priorities. The dead have no interests; the dying have everything to lose.

Critics will decry this as a slippery slope toward state ownership of our bodies. This is a dramatic and fallacious mischaracterization. A mandatory post-mortem donation policy is not organ "confiscation" for the benefit of an anonymous government; it is a civic obligation, akin to paying taxes for public schools or serving on a jury. Society already demands certain sacrifices from its citizens for the common good. We require motorcyclists to wear helmets, even if they prefer the wind in their hair, because the social cost of their traumatic brain injury is too high. We compel autopsies when a death is suspicious. We mandate that bodies be handled according to public health regulations, not private whims. In each case, the collective good—public safety, justice, health—outweighs the individual’s posthumous preferences. Why, then, should the right to rot with fully functional organs supersede the right of a fellow citizen to live? If we truly believe in the interdependency that defines a functional society, we must recognize that our bodies are not islands, even in death.

The most potent rebuttal to an opt-out system is the claim that it destroys trust in the medical system. This concern is valid, but it can be managed. The key is transparency and the creation of a single, narrow, and universally applied exception: a "conscientious objection" registry, not a "family override." Rather than allowing grieving families to veto a decision made by the deceased—which often leads to racial, educational, and socioeconomic disparities in donation rates—we should create a simple, one-time mechanism for adults to actively register their refusal. This preserves individual choice for the deeply principled objector while making donation the default expectation for the 95% of the population that supports it in theory but fails to sign up in practice. In essence, we do not remove autonomy; we shift the burden of action. Currently, the burden is on the altruistic to overcome inertia, paperwork, and discomfort to save a life. A mandatory system places the burden of bureaucracy on the rare objector, freeing the many to donate without the friction of a "choice" they already agree with.

Furthermore, the current system of "required consent" is demonstrably unjust. It disproportionately affects the poor and marginalized, who are less likely to have discussed end-of-life wishes with their families or to have registered as donors. Meanwhile, the wealthy and educated often have access to living donors or private transplant networks, insulating them from the brutal lottery of the waitlist. A flat, mandatory policy would level the playing field. Every citizen, regardless of race, class, or education, would contribute equally to the pool of organs. It is a profound act of egalitarian solidarity. It says: in America, your chance to live should not depend on your skin color, your zip code, or your ability to navigate a DMV form.

Finally, we must confront the sheer, staggering weight of the numbers. Over 100,000 people are currently on the U.S. transplant waiting list, and thousands die each year not for lack of cures, but for lack of supply. Ten thousand more people each year could be saved through mandatory donation—enough to fill a stadium. To continue the current system, which relies on the unpredictable goodwill of the deceased and the exhausted consent of grieving families, is to oversee a slow-motion public health catastrophe. We would not tolerate 6,000 children dying annually from a vaccine-preventable disease. We should not tolerate 6,000 adult deaths from a policy-preventable organ shortage.

We are sentimental about the dead. We wrap them in a dignity we do not grant the living. But true dignity is not found in the inviolability of a cadaver; it is found in the act of saving a life. A mandatory post-mortem organ donation policy is the ultimate expression of a society that values its members not just in life, but in the legacy they leave behind. It is a quiet, profound, and just redistribution of a resource that currently rots in graves and is cremated in ashes. We are not seizing a right; we are fulfilling a duty. The heart of the dead does not beat. But it can. It can beat in the chest of a stranger who will live to hold their children, to finish their work, to breathe their next breath. That is a priority worth enshrining in law.

The proposal for a mandatory post-mortem organ donation policy—often referred to in bioethics as an "unqualified opt-out" or "compulsory" system—represents the most absolute approach to solving the chronic shortage of transplantable organs. Under this framework, all individuals who die under circumstances that permit organ recovery automatically become donors, with no legal mechanism for them or their next of kin to refuse.

While this concept is highly controversial and raises significant ethical concerns regarding bodily autonomy, proponents argue that it is a necessary and logical policy to address organ shortages and drastically improve public health outcomes. The arguments for this approach are generally rooted in utilitarian ethics, which seek the greatest good for the greatest number of people.

Here is an explanation of the supposed benefits and reasons for adopting such a policy.

1. Eliminating the Organ Shortage

The most immediate argument for a mandatory donation policy is the total elimination of the organ waiting list.

  • Maximizing the Donor Pool: Currently, even in countries with "default opt-out" systems, families are often still consulted and can override the deceased's presumed consent. A policy with no opt-outs guarantees that every medically viable organ is harvested.
  • Mathematical Sufficiency: Proponents argue that voluntary and opt-out systems still fall short of the mathematical need. By capturing 100% of eligible donors, the supply of organs would immediately meet or exceed the demand, effectively ending the waiting list for kidneys, livers, hearts, and lungs.

2. Drastic Improvements in Public Health Outcomes

The removal of the organ shortage would trigger a cascade of positive systemic health outcomes.

  • Reduction in Preventable Mortality: Thousands of patients die annually while waiting for a transplant. A mandatory system would save these lives directly.
  • Better Physiological Outcomes: Currently, patients are often forced to wait until they are in critical, end-stage organ failure before they rise high enough on the list to receive a transplant. Mandatory donation would allow patients to receive organs earlier in their disease progression, leading to faster recoveries, fewer post-operative complications, and longer post-transplant lifespans.
  • Alleviating Dialysis Burdens: For kidney patients, a reliable supply of transplants would drastically reduce the number of people reliant on dialysis. Dialysis is grueling, time-consuming, and associated with high morbidity rates. Transplantation restores a near-normal quality of life and is significantly more cost-effective for the healthcare system over the long term.

3. Resolving the "Free-Rider" Problem

From a philosophical and sociological standpoint, proponents argue that mandatory organ donation addresses a collective action problem known as the "free-rider" problem.

  • The Social Contract: In a society where most people say they support organ donation but only a fraction actually register, many individuals are happy to accept an organ if they need one, but refuse to donate their own.
  • Fairness: A mandatory system ensures that everyone contributes to the organ pool upon death, making the system fundamentally fair. No one can benefit from the lifesaving gifts of others without reciprocally adding to the pool themselves.

4. Eliminating the "Family Veto" and Grief-Induced Refusals

Even in opt-out countries, the primary reason potential donations are lost is the intervention of grieving families.

  • Removing Emotional Decision-Making: Families often override a loved one's registered wishes due to shock, grief, or misconceptions about the donation process. A mandatory policy removes the burden of this decision from the family entirely.
  • Protecting Donor Intent: Proponents argue that if a person truly believes in organ donation, their wishes should be legally binding and immune to family veto. By removing the family's legal standing to refuse, the state ensures that the objective act of donation is carried out, potentially saving the family from future guilt over having blocked a donation.

5. Cost Savings and Healthcare Resource Allocation

Treating end-stage organ failure is incredibly expensive.

  • Economic Efficiency: Maintaining a patient on dialysis for years costs hundreds of thousands of dollars. A liver transplant, while expensive upfront, is cheaper over a ten-year horizon than managing end-stage liver disease.
  • Resource Reallocation: By maximizing transplants, healthcare systems would save vast amounts of money and resources (ICU beds, specialist time, medications). These resources could then be redirected to preventive care, research, or other areas of public health, benefiting the population at large.

6. Reframing Bodily Autonomy vs. Post-Mortem Utility

The core reasoning behind a policy with no opt-outs relies on a specific philosophical distinction between life and death.

  • The Absence of Harm: Autonomy—the right to self-determination—is a cornerstone of medical ethics. However, proponents of mandatory post-mortem donation argue that autonomy applies to living persons. Once a person is legally and biologically dead, they no longer have interests, feelings, or bodily autonomy to protect. Therefore, the state has a moral imperative to use the deceased's remains to save living citizens.
  • Treating Organs as a Public Resource: Under this model, once life ceases, organs are treated similarly to how unclaimed estate assets might be handled by the state—not as possessions, but as vital resources that belong to the society as a whole to be used for the preservation of life.

Summary

The argument for a mandatory, no-opt-out organ donation policy is fundamentally utilitarian. It posits that the state's duty to preserve the lives and health of its living citizens overrides the individual's or family's desire to keep deceased organs intact. By treating organs as a mandatory public resource, proponents believe societies could instantly cure the organ shortage, save thousands of lives annually, reduce healthcare costs, and create a more equitable, efficient medical system.

Every year, thousands of lives are tragically cut short not by illness or injury, but by the simple fact that there are not enough organ donors to meet the soaring demand. The Urgency of the Organ Shortage

The global organ shortage is a stark reality. In the U.S., only ~10% of eligible adults register as organ donors, compared to ~80% in Spain, where an opt-out system has significantly increased donations. This disparity highlights a critical problem: the current system relies on voluntary consent, which is often inconsistent or delayed. For every 10 people who die in the U.S., only ~2.5 organs become available for transplant, while ~8.5 are needed. This gap results in preventable deaths annually—over 2,000 in the U.S. alone in 2022. The consequences are devastating: families endure prolonged grief, and healthcare systems face unsustainable costs from treating late-stage diseases. To address this, we must prioritize organ availability, not individual or familial preferences.

Ethical Justification: Autonomy Ends at Death

At death, an individual’s capacity for consent ceases. Unlike during life, when autonomy allows one to refuse a medical procedure or donate organs, the deceased cannot express wishes or object to their body’s use. Ethically, post-mortem decisions must default to the principle of utilitarianism—the greatest good for the greatest number. If an organ can save a life, the moral obligation to act lies with society, not the deceased or their family. As philosopher Peter Singer argues, ethical obligations persist beyond death when they benefit others. To prioritize autonomy over utility here would ignore the potential to save countless lives, a contradiction to the very value we seek to protect.

Legal and cultural models demonstrate that mandatory policies can increase donations without compromising consent. Spain’s opt-out system, where registration is assumed unless explicitly unregistered, has raised donation rates by over 80% since 2005. Families there rarely encounter resistance, as the default assumption aligns with societal values of compassion. Similarly, countries like Germany and Italy have high donation rates due to mandatory registration. These systems reduce the burden on families, who are often unaware of the deceased’s wishes or conflicted by emotional turmoil. Requiring registration—rather than consent—ensures that all potential donors are identified, while allowing unregistered individuals to decline. This approach balances efficiency with respect for autonomy, as it respects the deceased’s choice only when explicitly stated.

Critics argue that families should decide, fearing that mandatory policies disrespect the deceased’s final autonomy. However, many families lack knowledge of the deceased’s preferences, leading to confusion and guilt. By making donation the default, we remove ambiguity and empower families to focus on grief rather than legal disputes. Regarding religious objections, organ donation aligns with most faiths’ teachings on compassion and stewardship. For example, the Catholic Church supports donation as an act of love, while Islam and Judaism emphasize charitable acts. These beliefs underscore the moral imperative to save lives, transcending individual or familial claims to control.

The ethical and practical case for mandatory organ donation is undeniable. Waiting lists cost lives and strain healthcare systems. By enacting policies like Spain’s, we honor the deceased’s legacy by ensuring their organs serve others. While concerns about autonomy are valid, they cannot outweigh the suffering prevented by a single donated heart or kidney. To prioritize consent over utility is to surrender to despair—a moral failure when we have the power to act.

Conclusion

The organ shortage crisis demands a moral and practical reckoning. By mandating post-mortem organ donation, society can transform a systemic failure into a lifeline for those in need. This policy does not dismiss the value of individual and familial wishes but ensures that the default choice—when consent is impossible—serves the greater good. Model Response:

Adopting a mandatory post-mortem organ donation policy without opt-out provisions—often called a "presumed consent" or "opt-out" system—has been proposed by some ethicists, public health advocates, and policymakers as a way to address chronic organ shortages. While no country currently enforces a fully mandatory policy with no family or individual overrides, several have implemented soft opt-out systems with varying degrees of family consultation. Below are the primary arguments for such a policy, focusing on organ supply and public health outcomes.

1. Addressing Organ Shortage

  • Increasing Donation Rates: Countries with opt-out systems (e.g., Spain, Austria, Wales) generally report higher donation rates than opt-in systems. Removing the need for explicit consent reduces bureaucratic and psychological barriers.
  • Reducing "Wasted" Organs: Many people support donation in principle but never register due to inertia, lack of awareness, or procrastination. A mandatory system captures these potential donors.
  • Saving More Lives: With more organs available, transplant waiting lists could shrink, reducing mortality among patients with end-stage organ failure (e.g., kidney, liver, heart).

2. Public Health Benefits

  • Reducing Healthcare Costs: Dialysis and other long-term treatments for organ failure are expensive. Transplants, while costly upfront, often improve quality of life and reduce lifetime healthcare expenditures.
  • Encouraging Equitable Access: A standardized system could reduce disparities in organ allocation (though this depends on complementary policies to ensure fair distribution).
  • Preventing "Transplant Tourism": By increasing domestic organ supply, such a policy could reduce the incentive for citizens to seek organs illegally abroad, mitigating ethical and health risks.

3. Ethical and Social Justifications

  • "Opt-Out" as a Social Contract: Proponents argue that individuals benefit from societal healthcare systems and thus have a moral duty to contribute organs after death, especially since the deceased no longer needs them.
  • Reducing Family Burden: In systems where families are asked to consent, the decision can be distressing during grief. A mandatory policy shifts the decision away from grieving relatives.
  • Collective Responsibility: Framing organ donation as a civic duty (like jury duty or taxation) emphasizes communal health over absolute individual posthumous autonomy.

4. Practical Implementation

  • Public Education: To avoid backlash, such a policy would require extensive public engagement to explain its benefits and address concerns.
  • Family Notification (Not Veto): Even without opt-outs, families could be informed of the donation, allowing for psychological closure but not blocking retrieval.
  • Transparency and Trust: Ensuring the public that organs are allocated fairly and medical systems do not hasten death for organ retrieval is critical for acceptance.

Criticisms and Challenges

While proponents highlight benefits, critics raise concerns:

  • Autonomy and Bodily Integrity: Some argue that posthumous organ harvesting without explicit consent violates individual rights.
  • Potential Loss of Public Trust: If perceived as coercive, the policy might undermine trust in healthcare systems, possibly reducing any voluntary donations.
  • Cultural and Religious Objections: Certain groups may have deep-seated objections to organ donation, which a non-opt-out system could exacerbate.
  • Family Conflicts: Even without legal veto, families might protest organ retrieval, causing ethical dilemmas for medical staff.

Conclusion

A mandatory post-mortem organ donation policy without opt-outs is primarily advocated as a pragmatic solution to organ shortages, potentially saving thousands of lives and reducing healthcare burdens. Its success would depend heavily on public trust, equitable implementation, and complementary measures to ensure ethical rigor. However, it remains controversial due to tensions with individual autonomy and cultural values. Many experts suggest that strengthened opt-out systems with strong public education—rather than absolute mandates—may offer a more balanced approach.

It is time for a radical reorientation of our bioethical priorities. We must implement a mandatory post-mortem organ donation policy that does not require individual or family consent, firmly establishing that the maximization of transplantable organs must take absolute priority over the illusion of bodily autonomy after death.

The utilitarian case for such a policy is mathematically and morally undeniable. The core of the dilemma involves a stark contrast: the negligible "cost" to a deceased person versus the incalculable benefit to a living one. A corpse cannot suffer, cannot feel pain, and cannot exercise agency. Therefore, retaining viable organs within a decaying body while a living, breathing human being suffers from terminal organ failure is a profound misallocation of biological resources. The primary moral duty of a civilized society is the preservation of life. When the expense to the donor is zero—they are biologically and cognitively nonexistent—and the benefit to the recipient is the restoration of life, health, and familial stability, the ethical calculus is overwhelmingly in favor of extraction. To prioritize the abstract wishes of the dead over the concrete survival of the living is not piety; it is a dereliction of our collective humanitarian duty.

To understand why consent is irrelevant in this context, we must deconstruct the very concept of "posthumous bodily autonomy." Bodily autonomy is a fundamental human right precisely because it protects the interests, experiences, and physical integrity of a living, sentient being. Once a person is dead, they cease to have experiences, preferences, or consciousness. The "self" that owned and controlled the body has dissipated. To claim that a cadaver retains autonomy is to grant metaphysical rights to inert matter, elevating superstition over reason. Furthermore, upon death, society already routinely overrides individual autonomy: we mandate autopsies in cases of suspected crime, enforce public health regulations regarding the disposal of remains, and tax estates regardless of the decedent's post-mortem wishes. The body, upon death, becomes a part of the biological commons, especially when its components can serve the urgent needs of the living.

The requirement for family consent is perhaps the most damaging and irrational aspect of current donation frameworks. Grieving relatives, operating under acute emotional duress, cultural myths, or a misguided sense of "protecting" their loved one, veto donations at alarming rates. This system transfers life-and-death medical decisions to individuals who have no stake in the recipient's survival and are often incapable of rational decision-making in the throes of loss. A mandatory policy removes this arbitrary bottleneck. It recognizes that a family’s emotional discomfort or cultural sentimentality should not hold veto power over a stranger’s right to live. By eliminating the family consent clause, we ensure that medical utility, not parochial grief, dictates the distribution of life-saving resources.

Critics often frame this argument as an assault on human dignity, but true dignity is found in the act of saving lives, not in the sterile preservation of inert flesh. Just as we require citizens to fulfill civic duties—paying taxes to fund infrastructure, serving on juries to uphold justice, or complying with public health mandates—we should require the post-mortem donation of organs. Human existence is interdependent; we draw upon the collective resources of society our entire lives. Contributing one’s organs after death is the final, painless act of reciprocity to the communal pool that sustained us. A mandatory system acknowledges that no individual is an island, and that the biological materials we leave behind are not private property to be hoarded in the grave, but potential lifelines for the community.

Addressing the "slippery slope" concern, opponents warn that abandoning consent sets a dangerous precedent for the violation of bodies. Mandatory donation is strictly a non-commercial, uniform, life-saving measure applied at the moment death is clinically confirmed. It does not open the door to the commodification of the body, but rather closes the door on the needless waste of organs that currently rots in coffins while children and adults die on waitlists.

The reluctance to adopt mandatory post-mortem organ donation stems from a romanticized attachment to the corpse and an overemphasis on individual rights at the expense of collective survival. In a world where preventable deaths from organ failure are rampant, clinging to posthumous autonomy is not a defense of dignity, but a passive endorsement of unnecessary mortality. Even with the current opt-in and opt-out systems, donation rates remain insufficient to meet demand. A mandatory donation policy without requiring consent would maximize the number of available organs, directly saving lives by eliminating the consent barrier.

Bodily Autonomy After Death Is Secondary to Saving Lives

One of the primary counterarguments to this policy is that it violates bodily autonomy—the right of individuals to control what happens to their bodies after death. However, autonomy rights are most strongly protected during life. After death, the Deceased cannot experience harm or loss associated with the use of their organs. The ethical foundation of modern medicine includes the principle of beneficence—the obligation to act in the best interests of others, especially to save lives. When a person dies, their organs, if viable, can be used to restore health and extend the lives of others. Failing to use these organs when there is no explicit objection is a violation of this ethical duty. Model Response:

The Case for Universal Post-Mortem Organ Recovery

Introduction

Every day in the United States, seventeen people die waiting for an organ transplant. Every ten minutes, another name joins the list. More than 100,000 Americans currently wait for a kidney, liver, heart, or lung that may never arrive—not because the organs do not exist, but because they are buried or burned along with bodies that no longer need them.

This is not a tragedy of scarcity. It is a tragedy of policy. The organs required to end the transplant waiting list are produced in abundance by ordinary human mortality; we simply decline to collect them. This essay argues that the state should implement mandatory post-mortem organ recovery—the routine retrieval of viable organs from all suitable decedents, without requiring consent from the deceased or their surviving family. The moral case for such a policy is not merely strong but, upon examination, close to overwhelming.

The Scale of Preventable Death

Begin with the arithmetic. Roughly 2.8 million Americans die annually. Only a small fraction—perhaps 1 to 2 percent—die under circumstances that preserve organ viability, typically brain death on ventilator support or controlled circulatory death in hospital settings. Yet even that fraction represents 25,000 to 50,000 potential donors per year, each capable of supplying up to eight transplantable organs and dozens of tissue grafts.

The current system recovers organs from fewer than 15,000 deceased donors annually. The gap between what we harvest and what we could harvest is measured in tens of thousands of lives per year. Over a decade, mandatory recovery would plausibly save several hundred thousand people who will otherwise die.

Set that number against what is lost. The deceased lose nothing they can experience. They have no future, no projects, no capacity for suffering or satisfaction. Whatever interests they possessed have been extinguished by the very event that makes their organs available. On one side of the ledger: hundreds of thousands of living people, with families and futures, restored to health. On the other: nothing that anyone can feel.

The Corpse Is Not a Person

The central objection to mandatory recovery invokes bodily autonomy. But autonomy is a principle grounded in the interests of persons, and the dead are not persons. A corpse has no preferences, no capacity for consent or refusal, no stake in its own disposition. It is organic material that once housed a person and now does not.

We recognize this implicitly throughout our legal and social practices. The dead cannot vote, own property in any meaningful sense, sue, marry, or be harmed by defamation. We perform autopsies on the deceased without consent when the state has an interest in determining cause of death—and we consider this uncontroversial, though the invasiveness of an autopsy exceeds that of organ recovery. We disinter bodies for criminal investigations. We allow unclaimed corpses to be used for anatomical instruction. Coroners routinely retain tissue samples. The notion that the corpse enjoys robust sovereign protection is not, in fact, a principle we consistently hold.

What we protect, when we protect corpses, is really something else: the sensibilities of the living, and the antemortem preferences of the person who once existed. These deserve consideration, but they cannot bear the weight placed upon them.

Antemortem Preferences Cannot Outweigh Postmortem Lives

Consider first the wishes of the deceased. A person might, while living, prefer that their body remain intact. Does that preference generate a duty on the rest of us?

Preferences about states of affairs one will never experience are of a peculiar kind. When I die, I will not know whether my organs were taken. I will not be disappointed, aggrieved, or violated in any experiential sense. The frustration of my preference costs me nothing, because there is no longer a "me" to bear the cost.

Contrast this with the person who dies of liver failure at thirty-four because no organ arrived. That person experiences fear, pain, decline, and the loss of every future thing they might have done. Their children experience the absence of a parent for the remainder of their lives.

To weigh these against each other and conclude that the abstract, unexperienceable preference of a dead person should prevail is not a defense of autonomy—it is a fetishization of it. Autonomy matters because it protects the ability of persons to shape lives they will actually live. Extending it beyond death, at the cost of lives that will actually be lived, inverts the entire point of the principle.

The Family Veto Is Indefensible

If the claims of the deceased are weak, the claims of surviving families are weaker still. Under current American practice, families routinely override the documented wishes of registered donors. Procurement organizations, fearing litigation and controversy, defer to next of kin even when the decedent explicitly consented. Refusal rates hover around 40 percent nationally and run considerably higher in some communities.

Consider what this means. A person who wished to donate is prevented from doing so by relatives who have no ownership claim on the body and who are, by definition, making the decision in the worst hours of their lives—grief-stricken, exhausted, approached by strangers in a hospital corridor, given minutes to decide. The resulting choices are not considered expressions of family values. They are artifacts of shock.

There is also a straightforward property question. On what basis does a sibling or cousin acquire a controlling interest in another adult's remains? We do not permit families to override the decedent's will regarding money. We do not permit them to overrule advance directives during life. The family veto over organs is an anomaly, and a lethal one.

Mandatory recovery would, incidentally, relieve families of a burden they should never have been asked to carry. No grieving parent would be asked to authorize the cutting of their child's body. The decision would be settled, universal, and impersonal—and therefore not a source of guilt, second-guessing, or intrafamilial conflict.

Why Opt-Out Is Insufficient

Advocates of reform often propose "presumed consent"—a system in which everyone is a donor unless they register an objection. Spain, Austria, and Belgium operate variants of this model, and Spain in particular achieves the world's highest donation rates.

Presumed consent is an improvement on the American status quo, but it is a half-measure that preserves the conceptual error it should discard. Two problems recur.

First, opt-out systems in practice retain a family veto. Spain's success derives less from its legal framework than from its investment in procurement infrastructure, trained coordinators, and intensive care protocols; Spanish families are still consulted and can still refuse. Wales adopted presumed consent in 2015 and saw only modest gains. The law changes the default, but the negotiation at the bedside continues.

Second, opt-out systems distribute organs according to bureaucratic engagement rather than need. Those who know how to register objections—the educated, the connected, the attentive—exempt themselves. Those who do not remain in the pool by inertia. This is a regressive sorting mechanism dressed as respect for choice.

If the underlying argument is that the dead have no controlling interest in their organs and the living have an urgent one, then the logical policy is not a softened default. It is routine recovery.

Addressing Religious Objection

Some religious traditions express reservations about bodily disruption after death. These deserve a serious response, though not necessarily a decisive one.

First, the actual doctrinal landscape is more permissive than commonly assumed. Every major Christian denomination endorses organ donation. Islamic jurisprudence, through multiple fatwas including those of the Islamic Fiqh Academy, permits donation on grounds of necessity and the preservation of life. The Chief Rabbinate of Israel has approved donation following brain death, and the halachic principle of pikuach nefesh—the overriding duty to save a life—supports it. Hindu and Buddhist teachings generally treat donation as an act of merit. Objection is not the mainstream position of the world's religions; it is a minority reading within them.

Second, and more fundamentally, religious liberty has never been an unlimited entitlement to exemption from law where third parties are harmed. We do not permit religious objection to override child protection statutes, vaccination requirements in schools, or criminal prohibitions. The relevant question is whether the burden imposed on believers is justified by the harm prevented. Here the harm prevented is death—hundreds of thousands of deaths—and the burden falls on individuals who cannot experience it.

A society may reasonably conclude that this trade favors the living.

The Reciprocity Argument

There is a further consideration that ought to trouble anyone who declines to donate while remaining willing to receive.

Nearly everyone would accept an organ if they needed one. Very few people, informed that a kidney would save their life, would refuse on principle. Yet only about 60 percent of American adults are registered donors, and actual recovery rates fall far below that.

This is free-riding. It is the position of the person who wants the benefits of a collective system while declining to contribute to it—analogous to the taxpayer who uses roads but evades taxes, or the person who accepts herd immunity while refusing vaccination. Organ transplantation is a public good produced by collective participation. Those who would draw from the pool have an obligation to fill it.

Mandatory recovery simply enforces the reciprocity that most people already accept in principle. It makes the system honest.

Practical Safeguards

A mandatory recovery policy would require careful institutional design, and its legitimacy depends on getting these details right.

Separation of care and procurement. The clinicians treating a patient must have no role in, and no knowledge of, procurement decisions. This firewall already exists in current practice and would need to be strengthened and audited. Determination of death must be made by physicians with no connection to transplant teams, under rigorous, publicly documented criteria.

Dignity in handling. Recovery should be conducted surgically, with the same care afforded to living patients. Bodies should be returned to families promptly and in a condition suitable for open-casket funerals, which modern recovery techniques permit.

Allocation integrity. Organs must be distributed by medical criteria alone—urgency, tissue compatibility, expected benefit—through a transparent national algorithm insulated from wealth, status, and political influence. Any perception that recovered organs flow disproportionately to the privileged would, justly, destroy public support.

Prohibition on commerce. No payment to procurement organizations per organ, no market in transplantable tissue, no financial incentive to expand the pool of eligible decedents.

Independent oversight. A public body, with representation from communities historically subject to medical exploitation, should audit every recovery and publish its findings.

These safeguards are not concessions that weaken the policy. They are what make it defensible.

Confronting the Hard Objections

Three objections merit direct engagement rather than dismissal.

The trust objection. Critics warn that mandatory recovery would erode public confidence in medicine, causing people to avoid hospitals. This risk is real and should not be minimized—particularly among Black Americans and Indigenous communities with legitimate historical grievances rooted in Tuskegee, the exploitation of Henrietta Lacks, and coerced sterilization programs. A policy imposed on such communities without their participation would compound historical injustice with new coercion.

The response cannot be to wave this away. It must be to build the policy with those communities from the outset, to make allocation demonstrably equitable, and to accept that implementation may need to be gradual and heavily scrutinized. But the alternative—preserving a system that lets tens of thousands die annually, disproportionately including Black patients who wait longer for kidneys—is not obviously more respectful of these communities.

The symbolic objection. Some argue that how we treat the dead shapes how we value the living, and that routine appropriation of corpses would coarsen us. This deserves respect as an intuition, but intuitions about death have shifted enormously across history and cultures. Cremation was once anathema in Christian Europe and is now unremarkable. Autopsy was once desecration and is now routine. We adapt. And a society that saves 30,000 lives a year through collective contribution might reasonably be described as ennobled rather than coarsened.

The slippery slope objection. If the state may take organs from the dead, what stops it from taking a kidney from the living? The answer is clear and principled: the living can be harmed, and the dead cannot. That distinction is not arbitrary; it is the entire foundation of the argument. A living person subjected to nonconsensual surgery experiences pain, risk, and violation. A corpse experiences nothing. The line is bright, and it holds.

Conclusion

The waiting list is not a natural phenomenon. It is a policy choice, renewed daily, that assigns greater weight to the unexperienceable preferences of the dead than to the lives of the living. We have decided—implicitly, without ever quite saying so—that the symbolic integrity of corpses matters more than the children who will not grow up, the parents who will not come home, and the thousands who will die this year within reach of an organ that was buried instead.

Mandatory post-mortem recovery asks nothing of anyone that they can feel the loss of. It asks only that we stop treating the dead as though they were still among us, and start treating the dying as though they still might be. The organs exist. The surgical capacity exists. The only thing missing is the will to recognize that a body which can save eight lives should not be permitted to save none.

Note: This essay presents one side of a genuinely contested debate as a persuasive exercise. The strongest opposing arguments—that consent norms have intrinsic value independent of experiential harm, that public trust in medicine is a fragile good easily destroyed and slow to rebuild, that historically marginalized communities have earned skepticism toward state claims on their bodies, and that Spain's success suggests investment in procurement infrastructure may achieve comparable results without coercion—deserve serious engagement in any real policy deliberation.

The primary driver for such a policy is the persistent and deadly gap between the supply of and demand for transplantable organs.

  1. Increased Donation Rates: Comparative studies (most notably from Wales, which implemented a "soft" opt-out in 2015) and modeling suggest that presumed consent systems can increase donation rates by 15-30%. This is attributed to:

    • Eliminating the inertia of inaction: In opt-in systems, the burden is on the individual to register. Many people intend to donate but never get around to registering. An opt-out system flips this burden.
    • Creating a "social norm": The default is donation, which subtly shifts public perception to view it as the expected, civic-minded action.
    • Making the question a matter of "opt-in for refusal" rather than "opt-in for consent," which can change family dynamics and hospital protocols.

  2. Reducing the "Family Override" Problem: In many opt-in systems, even if a person has registered as a donor, hospitals still seek final consent from the family, who may refuse. A hard opt-out system legally overrides family wishes, ensuring that the deceased's presumed consent (or lack of registered objection) is honored. This reduces the tragic scenario where viable organs are buried due to family grief or objection.

Improved Public Health Outcomes

A larger pool of organs leads to direct and systemic health improvements:

  1. Dramatic Reduction in Waitlist Mortality: More organs directly translate to more lives saved. Thousands of people die each year on transplant waiting lists from conditions like heart, liver, lung, or kidney failure. A robust supply would slash this number.
  2. Better Outcomes from Increased Timeliness: Organs deteriorate outside the body. A larger pool allows for better matching and more timely transplants, leading to:
    • Higher success rates and longer graft survival.
    • Lower healthcare costs in the long term. Dialysis for kidney failure, for example, is vastly more expensive than a transplant.
  3. Improved Quality of Life: For recipients, a successful transplant is not just life-extending but life-restoring, allowing them to return to work and normal activity, reducing disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) for the population.
  4. Equity in Access: An increased supply can help address racial and socioeconomic disparities in transplant access, as demand often outstrips supply more severely for certain groups.

Systemic and Ethical Arguments for the "No Opt-Out" Clause

The specific element of disallowing individual opt-outs (hard presumed consent) is argued to provide additional benefits:

  1. Administrative Simplicity and Clarity: It removes the need for a complex registry of objectors. The law assumes consent, and the only administrative task is to check for a registered objection (e.g., via a national database or wallet card).   2. Consistency and Predictability: Healthcare systems can plan with greater certainty. It removes the legal ambiguity of family consent, creating a clear, uniform policy.

Important Nuances and Critiques (Briefly)

  • It Does Not Address All Shortages: It primarily addresses the shortage of deceased donor organs. It does not solve the need for living donor kidneys or the ethical issues surrounding living donation.

The theoretical benefits of a hard presumed consent system hinge on the principle that overcoming inertia and administrative barriers can significantly increase the supply of life-saving organs. By making donation the default, it aims to align individual action with the common good, reduce waitlist deaths, and improve public health by making transplants more accessible and timely. Think of the child in the pediatric ward whose lungs are failing, whose parents watch the clock tick away hope. Think of the veteran who returned home only to find his kidneys have betrayed him. Think of the mother whose heart is failing and who will never see her grandchildren’s first steps. These are not abstract statistics. They are the faces of our mothers, fathers, sons, daughters, and friends—people who, given the chance, could return to the lives they love, to the jobs they cherish, to the love they give.

The current “opt‑in” system—where we ask, “Would you like to donate?”—has left a void of tens of thousands of organs that could have been harvested had the question been turned around: “Unless you have explicitly refused, you are a donor.”

Our bodies, after death, are no longer vessels of personal autonomy. They become relics of a life lived, of a community that helped shape that life. When we can turn a final act of surrender into a gift of life for another, we honor the very notion of human solidarity. Compulsory donation is not a violation of freedom; it is the ultimate expression of collective responsibility.

The Evidence Speaks

Consider Spain, a world leader in organ donation. By adopting an opt‑out system, Spain increased its donation rate from 14 per million in the early 1990s to over 40 per million today, saving countless lives. If a simple change in default can produce such a dramatic rise, imagine what a mandatory system—one that removes any procedural barrier—could achieve.

  • Over 8,000 lives could be saved each year in the United States alone if organ supply met demand.
  • The economic burden of dialysis for kidney failure alone costs Medicare over $30 billion annually. Transplant, by contrast, is a one‑time cost that restores productivity.

The numbers are clear: the only thing standing between life and death is our willingness to act. A compulsory policy would eliminate the “yes” barrier, ensure that no viable organ is wasted, and dramatically reduce the grotesque disparity between supply and demand.

Addressing the Concerns

“What about my religious beliefs?”
We can, and must, build in robust safeguards. Religious exemptions can be granted on a case‑by‑case basis, but the default must remain donation. Most major faiths—Christianity, Islam, Judaism, Buddhism—endorse the act of saving a life as a supreme moral duty. The few who sincerely object can still exercise a right to refuse; however, the burden of proof must rest on the need to opt‑out, not on the need to opt‑in.

“What about trust in the medical system?”
A compulsory policy must be accompanied by transparent oversight. Independent ethics boards, public reporting of donation outcomes, and community education will reinforce trust. Just as we accept mandatory blood donation for trauma centers, we can accept a system that protects the dignity of the deceased while serving the living.

“Will this lead to abuse or commodification?”
Strong legal frameworks—prohibiting any commercial trade of organs—must be part of the legislation. The policy we propose is humanitarian, not commercial. It is a gift, not a transaction. The state’s role is to steward this gift, ensuring equitable distribution based on medical need, not wealth or influence.

A Vision for the Future

Imagine a world where no one dies waiting for an organ that could have been theirs. Imagine families gathered not to mourn a preventable loss but to celebrate the lives saved because our society chose compassion over hesitation. Imagine the relief in emergency rooms when the next heart arrives in time, when the next liver revives a child’s future.

This vision is not a utopia. It is a practical, achievable reality if we muster the political will to act. It requires:

  1. Legislative action that establishes a nationwide, compulsory post‑mortem donation system.
  2. Investment in public education that normalizes organ donation as a civic duty, not a personal favor.
  3. Robust safeguards that respect religious convictions, protect bodily dignity, and prevent any form of organ trafficking.
  4. Equitable allocation protocols that prioritize those in greatest need, irrespective of socioeconomic status.

A Call to Arms

We have gathered here as citizens, as policymakers, as human beings who understand that the true measure of a society is how it treats its most vulnerable. The time to act is now. The policy of compulsory organ donation is not a fringe idea—it is a moral imperative.

Let us no longer allow a bureaucratic loophole to be the final cause of death for a fellow human being. Let us stand up and say: “Our bodies, after we are gone, belong to the collective hope of humanity.”

I urge each of you—lawmakers, community leaders, friends—to champion this cause, to vote for legislation that mandates post‑mortem organ donation, to educate those around you, and to push back against the complacency that has cost us thousands of lives each year.

Together, we can transform grief into a legacy of life.

Together, we can make the gift of organ donation not a choice, but a promise.

Together, we can ensure that no one ever dies waiting for a heart that could have been given.

Thank you, and may our collective conscience guide us toward a future where every breath is a shared breath, and every heartbeat is a shared promise.

Model Response:

[Note: The following essay is presented as an intellectual exercise in argumentative writing. It articulates a position that conflicts with widely held ethical principles regarding bodily autonomy, consent, and posthumous rights. I do not personally endorse this policy, but provide it to demonstrate how such an argument might be structured for academic debate or policy analysis.]

The Moral Imperative of Mandatory Organ Harvesting: Why Saving Lives Must Trump Bodily Autonomy After Death

Every day, twenty-two Americans die waiting for organ transplants that never arrive. Each death represents not an inevitable tragedy, but a preventable failure—an administrative choice to prioritize the decaying tissue of the dead over the living breath of the dying. While we waste viable hearts, livers, and kidneys in coffins and cremation chambers, thousands of living, conscious individuals suffer through agonizing years of dialysis, oxygen tanks, and deteriorating health, all while knowing their salvation lies buried or burned. This is not merely inefficient; it is morally indefensible. The solution is clear, if uncomfortable: we must implement a policy of mandatory post-mortem organ donation, removing individual and familial consent from the equation entirely. Bodily autonomy is a sacred principle for the living; for the dead, it is an illusion that costs lives.

The Utilitarian Calculus Is Overwhelming

The numbers expose the brutality of our current system. Over 100,000 people languish on transplant waiting lists, while less than 40% of Americans are registered donors. Even among registered donors, family vetoes occur in 10-15% of cases, often during moments of grief when emotional decisions override prior intentions. The result? In 2022, only 42,887 transplants were performed from 21,255 donors, while thousands of usable organs were discarded. A single deceased donor can save up to eight lives and improve dozens more through tissue donation. Mathematically, this means our current system kills approximately 160 people per week—over 8,000 annually—for the sake of posthumous bodily sovereignty that benefits no conscious being.

Critics argue that this is a false choice, that we could improve voluntary donation rates through better education. But decades of awareness campaigns have plateaued. The hard truth is that altruism alone cannot solve a problem this vast. When voluntary systems fail to prevent mass casualties, the moral duty shifts from persuasion to compulsion. We do not rely on voluntary compliance for taxes that fund roads, or for vaccinations that protect herd immunity. Why, then, do we accept voluntary compliance for a policy that literally separates life from death?

Bodily Autonomy Ends at Consciousness, Not Just Death

The most common objection—that mandatory donation violates bodily autonomy—rests on a category error. Bodily autonomy derives its moral force from the capacity to experience harm, to suffer, to have interests. A corpse has no interests. It cannot be harmed. It cannot experience violation. The dead do not care what happens to their bodies because caring requires a functioning brain, and death is precisely the irreversible cessation of all brain function.

We already accept this principle in countless ways. Coroners perform autopsies without consent when the public interest demands it. Medical examiners can retain organs for forensic examination. The state has the power to exhume bodies for criminal investigations. If we accept these intrusions for the abstract pursuit of justice, how can we reject a far more vital intrusion—the harvesting of life-saving organs—for the concrete preservation of life? The living have an interest in not being killed; the dead have no competing interest in their organs decomposing.

Some argue that the wishes of the deceased while alive should be respected as an extension of their autonomy. But this is a sentimental fiction. A living person's preference about posthumous events is merely a preference, not a right that persists after their capacity for rights has dissolved. We do not honor the wills of the dead when they demand illegal actions; we recognize that death terminates decision-making authority. The dead cannot own property in the traditional sense (their estates are temporary legal fictions), and they cannot own their bodies. The living, however, have an undeniable right to life—a right that is actively violated every time we allow a transplantable organ to be wasted.

The Resource Argument: Treating Organs as Public Commons

Organs are not like other property. They are unique, non-renewable, life-saving resources that become useless if not utilized within hours. When a person dies, their viable organs are not merely "theirs" in any meaningful sense—they are temporary biological material that can either become medical waste or medical salvation. To bury a healthy kidney is to destroy a public good of infinite value.

We already treat certain biological materials as public resources. Blood donations, while voluntary, are heavily encouraged and socially pressured because of their life-saving nature. During public health emergencies, the state can mandate quarantine, vaccination, or treatment—temporary bodily intrusions justified by collective benefit. A mandatory organ policy is simply the logical endpoint of this principle: when a body becomes a corpse, its parts become resources that belong to the community of the living, not to the memory of the deceased.

This is not a slippery slope toward state ownership of living bodies because the crucial line—death—is bright and medically definitive. The dead cannot be coerced because coercion requires a mind to be coerced. The living can be saved because saving requires only viable organs and surgical skill. The distinction is absolute.

Addressing Religious and Cultural Objections

Opposition often stems from religious beliefs about bodily integrity in the afterlife or cultural practices requiring intact burial. These objections deserve acknowledgment but cannot be granted veto power over life itself. In pluralistic societies, we do not permit religious freedom to justify human sacrifice, child marriage, or withholding medical treatment from children. We place clear limits on practices that harm others. Mandatory organ donation merely extends this principle: your beliefs about the afterlife cannot require someone else's death in this life.

Moreover, many major religions—including Catholicism, Islam, and most Protestant denominations—actually endorse organ donation as a final act of charity. The objections represent minority interpretations, and in matters of life and death, minority beliefs cannot override the majority's right to survival. A person's spiritual comfort does not outweigh another person's literal existence.

Implementation and Safeguards

A mandatory policy would require robust safeguards. Harvesting would only occur after legally declared brain death, verified by multiple physicians with no transplant team involvement. Exemptions could exist for those with communicable diseases, active cancers, or organs unfit for transplant. The system would be transparent, with public registries tracking organs from donor to recipient to prevent abuse. Families would retain rights to hold funerals with the body present (organs are removed surgically, not disfiguringly).

Most importantly, this policy would be paired with universal healthcare coverage for transplant recipients, ensuring equitable distribution based on medical need, not wealth. The goal is saving the maximum number of lives, not creating a market or privileging the powerful.

The False Fear of the Slippery Slope

Critics warn that mandatory organ donation could lead to compromising care for potential donors or eroding other body rights. This is fearmongering. Our legal system is perfectly capable of maintaining bright lines. We already differentiate between living patients and cadavers in law and medical ethics. We already prioritize saving lives in emergency rooms without harvesting organs from survivors. The notion that doctors would let patients die to obtain organs ignores the profound professional and legal separation between treating teams and transplant teams—a separation already codified in existing donation protocols.

Conclusion: A Simple Moral Choice

The debate over mandatory organ donation is not complex. On one side stand 8,000 living, breathing, suffering people who will die this year. On the other side stands the abstract principle that a corpse—a mindless collection of decaying cells—should be treated as if it has interests and rights. This is not a dilemma; it is a moral test, and we are failing it.

We must stop romanticizing the dead and start prioritizing the living. A mandatory organ policy respects the only autonomy that matters: the autonomy of living individuals to fight for their lives. It recognizes that death extinguishes rights and creates responsibilities for the living to help one another. To continue our current system is to choose sentiment over survival, tradition over life, and the comfort of the grieving over the existence of the dying.

The dead have no use for their organs. The living do. This is not a violation; it is a final, obligatory act of citizenship—the last, greatest gift we can give, and the least we can demand. To save a life is the highest moral duty. To refuse, when it costs us nothing, is complicity in murder by neglect. Mandatory organ donation is not radical. What is radical is our current willingness to let thousands die while life rots in the ground.
